reason: The text of Ruth clearly demonstrates significant agency exercised by non-leaders. Ruth, a poor foreign widow with no official status, takes multiple decisive actions: she initiates gleaning in the fields ('אֵֽלְכָה־ נָּ֤א הַשָּׂדֶה֙'), she boldly approaches Boaz at the threshing floor, and her own character and initiative drive the resolution of the narrative. Similarly, Naomi—an older widow without husband or sons—demonstrates substantial agency in planning the threshing floor encounter and advising Ruth. Even Orpah exercises agency in choosing to return to her people. The narrative emphasizes Ruth's 'חֵן' (favor/grace) stemming from her own character and actions, not from any leadership position. Boaz, while a man of means and status, must defer to legal procedures and other community members, and he is often responding to Ruth's agency rather than directing events. The story fundamentally centers on marginalized women whose resourcefulness and determination resolve the crisis, contradicting the notion that only leaders possess agency.
